In Mary's River, it falls on the first syllable of a stem; in Tualatin and Yoncalla, stress is often shifted to prefixed elements. If a prefix is added in Mary's River, stress does not move: waú·tso?, kuwaú·tso?. Stress is accompanied generally by higher pitch (sometimes perhaps by lower pitch), which Jacobs calls "pitch accent." He says that pitch accent falls on "every syllable felt to be an independent root--nominal, pronominal, connective, or verbal" (1930: n.p.). Since stress is not always predictable from the segmental construction alone, it is considered to be phonemic." new_statements.rule_in_words: Kalapuyan generally has a (pitch-)accent on the first syllable of the root/stem (so described first-hand for Mary's River and Santiam Central Kalapuya). For Tualatin (Northern Kalapuya) the only accessible statements are incidental comparative remarks in these Central-Kalapuya theses: stress is 'often shifted to prefixed elements' (Hajda), i.e. with a short monosyllabic root the stress lands on the preceding (prefix) syllable = the penult of the word (Lewis). No full rule for Tualatin is given; the system looks root-based with weight-conditioned retraction, but this is not worked out in any source I could open.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Tualatin. (Lewis 2003:63 fn.14, for Central Kalapuya: secondary stress on the left-most syllabic nucleus of pronominals/adverbials.)
new_statements.exceptions: Lewis: monosyllabic short roots take penultimate (prefix) stress; roots with 'variable vowels' may be long anyway. Hajda: shift to prefixes is 'often', not always.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress/pitch accent as marked in Frachtenberg's and Jacobs' text transcriptions (connected texts, not citation forms); Hajda treats stress as phonemic and accompanied by higher pitch (Jacobs' 'pitch accent'). Both remarks about Tualatin are made in passing in descriptions of Central Kalapuya varieties (Mary's River; Santiam), based on Frachtenberg/Jacobs manuscripts and Berman's Tualatin slip files from Louis Kenoyer.
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted remarks concern the Tualatin (Tfalati/Atfalati, 'Twalatin') dialect of Northern Kalapuya as recorded from Louis Kenoyer and earlier Gatschet/Frachtenberg consultants; nothing was found on the Yamhill dialect. The host works describe Central Kalapuya varieties (Mary's River and Santiam, glottocode kala1402 'Kalapuya' / Central Kalapuya [kyl]); their Tualatin statements are comparative asides, not a description of tual1242 in its own right. Hajda groups Tualatin with Yoncalla (Southern Kalapuya, sout2964) as both showing stress shift onto prefixes.

sources.note: Suprasegmentals p.45: stress independent of length; in Mary's River (Central Kalapuya) it falls on the first syllable of a stem and does not move when a prefix is added; 'in Tualatin and Yoncalla, stress is often shifted to prefixed elements'; accompanied by higher pitch (Jacobs' 'pitch accent', which per Jacobs 1930 ms falls on 'every syllable felt to be an independent root'); considered phonemic. Summary p.49-50: 'Phonemic stress occurs on the first syllable of stems'.
